previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A 30-year-old woman with Type 1 diabetes and a history of gastroparesis s/p gastric pacer presented with acute nausea and vomiting, one week after a prior hospitalization for similar symptoms. She had recently received a Botox injection for gastroparesis and noticed dark material in her vomit, likely due to a Mallory-Weiss tear. She was admitted for inability to tolerate oral intake and managed with bowel rest, IV fluids, and antiemetics including Zofran, Reglan, and Ativan. A nasogastric tube was placed in the ED but removed by the patient. Her symptoms improved gradually, allowing advancement to a soft diet. Labs showed mild metabolic acidosis and stable hemoglobin, with no evidence of ongoing bleeding. She was discharged home in stable condition on her prior medications with follow-up planned in gastroenterology and primary care.
problems: Diabetes with neurological manifestations, type I [juvenile type], uncontrolled

Brief Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with nausea and vomiting (not 
tolerating pos) after recent discharge for diabetic 
gastroparesis.  She was given IV hydration, IV protonix, reglan, 
compazine, zofran and diazepam and improved clinically to the 
point of tolerating pos including all medications.  Two KUBs 
were performed to rule out ileus vs. SBO in the setting of 
constipation, which were negative for obstipation.  She also had 
hypertension in the setting of vomiting and anxiety, which 
improved with IV metoprolol.  She was transitioned to po 
lisinopril (similar to prior regimen).  A ___ consult was 
called to evaluate her DM1 control, and her home regimen of 28U 
glargine + sliding scale humalog was considered adequate.  Her 
blood sugars were generally well controlled while she was 
hospitalized.

On the day of discharge the patient was hyponatremic to 130, and

radiology_notes.text:
REASON FOR EXAM:  ___ female with vomiting.  Clinical concern for
bowel obstruction.

COMPARISON:  Multiple abdominal radiographs with the most recent from ___, and CT abdomen and pelvis from ___.

TWO VIEWS OF THE ABDOMEN IN SUPINE AND ERECT POSITIONS:  The nasogastric tube
has been removed.  A gastric pacer device with leads overlying the left upper
quadrant is in stable position.  There is no pneumoperitoneum.  Stool within
the colon is identified.  Bowel gas pattern is nonspecific.  There are no soft
tissue calcifications.  Visualized osseous structures are grossly
unremarkable.

IMPRESSION:   No pneumoperitoneum.  Nonspecific bowel gas pattern.

INDICATION:  History of diabetic gastroparesis, rule out SBO versus ileus.

TECHNIQUE:  Frontal radiographs of the abdomen with the patient in erect and
supine positions.

COMPARISON:  Abdominal radiograph available from ___.

FINDINGS:  A gastric stimulator is present, with the generator unit located at
the right lower quadrant.  The leads appear intact.  Included views of the
chest are unremarkable.  The bowel gas pattern is within normal limits.  A
moderate amount of stool is present throughout the colon.  There is no free
air.  There is no acute fracture or dislocation.

IMPRESSION:  No evidence of ileus or small-bowel obstruction.  No free air.
